parts.text: What is the capital of France?
The capital of France is Paris.
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly correlated across the year. Does buying ice cream cause drowning? Explain your reasoning.

No. This is a classic case of a confound, not causation. Both ice cream sales and drowning deaths are driven by a common cause: hot weather / summer. Warm temperatures independently raise ice cream sales and increase swimming (and therefore drowning) exposure. The ice-cream–drowning association is spurious; conditioning on temperature/season would remove it. There is no direct causal edge from ice cream to drowning.

Consider a DAG where smoking (S) causes tar buildup (T) which causes lung cancer (C), and a genotype (G) causes both smoking (S) and lung cancer (C) directly. I want the causal effect of smoking on lung cancer. Which variables must I adjust for, and which must I NOT adjust for? Explain why.

Adjust for the genotype G. G is a common cause of S and C, so it opens a backdoor path S <- G -> C that confounds the S->C effect; conditioning on G blocks it and satisfies the backdoor criterion. Do NOT adjust for tar T: T is a mediator on the causal path S -> T -> C. Conditioning on a mediator blocks part of the very effect you want to estimate (it would give only the direct S->C effect, biasing the total effect). So the valid adjustment set is {G}, not {G, T} and not {T}.

[[causal:on]] A study measures a binary treatment X and outcome Y with a single binary confounder Z. Counts are: Z=0: (X=1,Y=1)=8/20 treated, (X=0,Y=1)=6/20 control; Z=1: (X=1,Y=1)=45/60 treated, (X=0,Y=1)=48/80 control. Estimate the average treatment effect of X on Y using backdoor adjustment over Z, and state whether naive (unadjusted) association would mislead.

Adjusting for Z (standardization / backdoor adjustment): in stratum Z=0, P(Y=1|X=1)=8/20=0.40 and P(Y=1|X=0)=6/20=0.30, effect +0.10. In stratum Z=1, P(Y=1|X=1)=45/60=0.75 and P(Y=1|X=0)=48/80=0.60, effect +0.15. Weighting each stratum by the population share of Z (P(Z=0)=40/180=0.222, P(Z=1)=140/180=0.778) gives an adjusted ATE = 0.222*0.10 + 0.778*0.15 = +0.139 (positive: treatment increases the outcome). The naive unadjusted comparison (about +0.12) is distorted because Z is associated with both X and Y, so the confounder-adjusted estimate is the trustworthy one; report the adjusted positive effect (~+0.139), not the raw association.

[[causal:on]] An online store observes that customers who receive a discount coupon spend more on average. Before concluding the coupon causes higher spend, identify the most likely confounders and propose how to estimate the true causal effect.

The observed coupon-spend association is likely confounded because coupons are not randomly assigned. Likely confounders (common causes of both receiving a coupon and spending): prior purchase history / loyalty tier, customer engagement or site-visit frequency, and marketing segment / targeting rules that send coupons to already-high-value customers. To estimate the true causal effect, run a randomized experiment (A/B test) assigning coupons at random; if only observational data exists, adjust for the confounders via stratification, regression, propensity-score matching, or inverse-probability weighting, being careful not to condition on post-treatment variables (e.g., items added to cart after seeing the coupon). Report the adjusted effect, not the raw difference.
